Passion isn’t a pond. It’s a current.

There’s always talk about the relationship between career and passion: how to align them, and how to find fulfillment in work. Some people treat passion as a fixed destination. Others see their career as simply a means to an end.

Especially for young professionals, there’s pressure to "figure it out" early. Find what you love, then build the perfect career around it. But it doesn’t have to be that rigid.

I’m not saying you don’t plan. But sometimes, it’s better to follow where life pulls you than to force a direction it’s resisting.

For me, the pull toward software hasn’t come from one single reason. It’s been a combination of forces.

 I can point to a love of problem-solving that is rooted in math.
 I can point to the satisfaction of building things that feel real.
 I can point to figuring things out on the computer at two... and not stopping since.

But more than anything, what keeps pulling me forward is my love of learning.

The deeper I dive into AI, into systems built to learn, the more it reinforces what I love about learning.

There’s something almost paradoxical about it. Studying machines designed to learn only makes me more aware of how much I still have to learn. The beauty of learning has always been in its lifelong process.

And somehow, that realization has never discouraged me. It energizes me.

Understanding how systems grow, adapt, and improve only deepens my drive to do the same.

Is it challenging? Definitely.
Is it scary sometimes? Sure.
But is it invigorating? Absolutely.

Passion isn’t a destination or a roadblock.

Passion is a current that pulls and carries you forward. You just have to trust and ride the flow.

Here’s what I think people undervalue when talking about creating prompts:

There’s a lot of talk these days about LLM “efficiency.” I see posts on my feed from time to time about “life hack” prompts and so-called “super prompts” that everyone needs to use.

And to be fair, some of those have taught me a thing or two. I’ve picked up inspiration here and there that I've applied to both personal and work-related use cases.

But what often gets overlooked is this:

Context. Always. Matters.

In any creative medium, whether it’s code, music, or visual art, there’s always a voice: a set of patterns shaped by personal, cultural, and historical background.

It’s no different with AI.

Whether we realize it or not, we each interact with language models in unique ways. From our tone to our phrasing, from what we ask to how we interpret results, we bring our own habits into the conversation.

Which means what works for one person might not work for you.

Take software as an example.

Can you generate bug-free, best-practice code with a prompt? Absolutely.

But can you ensure your output aligns with a codebase that spans many interconnected files and abstracted logic?

That’s another story.

That’s why these super prompts don’t always click with me.

You can write better prompts. You can have that clear and well-intended framework. But if you aren’t able to adapt it to your circumstances, the result won’t reflect what you need.

So next time you use a tool like ChatGPT, don’t just think about the result.

Think about the multi-layered conditions it would take to get there.

#PromptEngineering #ArtificialIntelligence #WorkSmarter #SoftwareDevelopment #LanguageModels

Adapting is about how you step forward, not how you step away.

A continuous mindset sees learning not only as a means to think, but a means to adapt.

In today's fast world, the ability to retain and apply your skills is crucial in an ever-changing environment.

People are constantly adjusting to new habits, new environments, and switching companies.

There is a further emphasis on upcycling skill sets, expanding abilities beyond your work environment.

But I think what people seem to leave out is the whole pivot when it comes to adapting.

Adapting does not mean uprooting; it means to shift.

Take software, for example.

Are there new frameworks coming out all the time? Yes.

Do new frameworks reinvent the wheel on what we constitute software development? No.

Frameworks build on what is already there. 

You can't let go of the foundation that already exists. It's that knowledge foundation of the past that solves problems in the present.

You don't solve a system with a new framework; you solve it with your proven fundamentals.

So that's why when you're learning something, never accept it alone, accept it as a part of your whole story.

#Adaptability #ContinuousLearning #LifelongLearning #GrowthMindset #SkillDevelopment

One thing conscious learning makes clear: transferable skills matter more than we think.

The ability to take apart any domain and make it a part of your own is a skill that pays off in unexpected places.

We all have that subject in school that we look back on less fondly than others. As for mine, that was history.

It’s not that I never liked history. I recount various names, events, and policies bouncing around my mind.

But piecing it all together into a concise, clear, analytical paper? That came with growing pains.

However, just because I’m not a history scholar does not mean I don’t apply history in day-to-day work.

Looking through large documentation? That is research.

Clear communication of technical concepts? That is analytical writing.

Breaking apart large software systems? That is cause and effect.

I may not have excelled at history, but that doesn’t mean I can’t appreciate its skills.

At the end of the day, there are no STEM people or liberal arts people. 

There is just that. People. Learning and growing in their own unique ways

So always be open to other disciplines. A greater perspective is what leads to greater knowing.

#ContinuousLearning #CareerGrowth #InterdisciplinaryThinking #ProfessionalDevelopment #LearningMindset

We strive for neutral AI. But is it ever truly neutral?

AI runs on large amounts of training data.

Training datasets are primarily created with the intent of keeping outputs as objective as possible.

Even though we strive to make things objective, there are always concealed biases.

Think about how datasets get formed.

They are not entirely out of randomness. 

Someone decides the priorities.

Someone decides what gets pushed through and what makes the cut.

Curating the dataset makes certain ideas more pronounced than others.

In turn, consider the current understanding of AI and LLMs.

By feeding in more pronounced patterns, you are going to get more pronounced responses.

These pronounced responses are not just the work of one.

They are the work of many people’s biases imprinted in the data, working to affect the outcome.

Thus, when we consider neutrality, we must examine the factors that introduce bias.

There are objective facts, but they always get filtered through the human perspective.

However, that is not to say bias is an inherent evil. 

Bias is always present. We can’t escape it. We just can’t let bias cloud our judgment.

Therefore, AI neutrality can be relative to human neutrality. Plausible on the surface, but impossible in reality.

#ArtificialIntelligence #AI #MachineLearning #LLM #TechThoughts

The key to any successful AI agent system? Understanding. Your. Personas.

Understanding personas is important to maintaining a proficient and consistent workflow.

But how do you design a multi-agent system around personas?

First, start at the goal. What is the overarching principle all these agents connect to?

Agents should be relevant to the steps you need to take in order to reach the output.

Once you’ve established the higher-level overview of the workflow, you need to develop each agent's boundaries.

Agent boundaries establish what knowledge each agent handles, what the special use cases are, and how to format the output.

As well, agent boundaries need to consider the granular and higher-level order of the workflow.

You need to consider how one agent connects to another.

As well, it’s critical to understand how an agent’s output connects with non-agent elements like a database or the human viewing the results.

And remember, AI agents work best when focused on a singular task.

Use a sniff test: can you describe an agent in 1 sentence at a non-technical level? If not, consider reevaluating your workflow.

AI agents are a powerful tool for an ambiguous workflow. With enough finetuning, agents can be configured to whatever setup your heart desires.

#ArtificialIntelligence #WorkflowOptimization #TechStrategy #Automation #AIAgents

AI responses should reflect the need, not the desire for the outcome.

There is a lot of discussion regarding the outputs of AI.

Especially in the context of detecting AI writing, everyone is looking for the leaves, but failing to understand the trees underneath.

Take the association between em dashes and AI usage, for example.

What is a simple convenience in formal writing is now an alarm bell for AI-generated text.

But why do people make that connection?

It isn’t because em dashes are archaic.

It is because AI is trained on a disproportionate amount of them.

Books, essays, and all these other formal pieces of writing often conflict with the language used in day-to-day life.

AI’s fixations on certain patterns highlight the push and pull in how language works.

AI perpetuates em dashes as a default.

Fewer people use them so as not to be seen as AI.

This reduces em dashes in future training data and, in turn, their use by LLMs.

Push and pull language loops aren't just seen in AI. Think about language adoption through slang, memes, and pop culture. 

Language doesn’t change because we desire it to; it changes because of external needs to process words. 

AI responses aren’t just about the results, but the feelings surrounding those results.

Here are ways AI workflows should follow how humans approach work:


1. Specialist over generalist 

While there are arguable tradeoffs to being a generalist able to adapt to a variety of scenarios, depth helps tackle problems more effectively than breadth.

Structured, specialized workflows enable AI to tackle one thing efficiently as opposed to many things at once. Modular assembly work is the primary benefit of AI agent systems as opposed to using a single LLM.

2. Clarity isn’t universal

What may make sense to you doesn’t always make sense to everyone else. Just like we are always trying to pick apart context, AI agents need an appropriate background to pick up patterns.

Clear instructions, examples, and boundaries are crucial to avoid errors and misinterpretations. Just like collaborating in the workplace, collaborating with AI helps identify which instructions are clear and which need refinement

3. Innovation doesn’t happen overnight

AI may accelerate productivity, but that doesn’t mean crashing the project into a wall. We always need to be planning, reflecting on what works, and taking consistent measures so we know exactly where it needs to be. Like any process, AI workflows grow with enough time, patience, and effort.

#ArtificialIntelligence #AIWorkflows #ContinuousLearning #TechWisdom #ProblemSolving

Most people misunderstand AI workflows. Here’s the reality:

AI agents are amazing at handling complex problems. 

They deal with things autonomously and can explore ambiguity in problems.

But just because an agent system can tackle complexity does not mean your problem is AI complex.

What I mean by this is rather than overengineering a system, you need to consider what fits the role of an agent and what can be achieved with lines of code.

If you can pinpoint all responses from an agent, it can be reduced to code.

When conditions change, an agent helps adapt to the needs of the output logic.

If the output is too simplistic and predictable, a simple API call would better suit the interaction.

You also need to consider the context of your interaction. The task type can be agent-based or not, depending on intent.

Take researching, for example:

If you are pulling from a predefined source, you can fetch document chunks with a function.

But pulling research from the internet? That’s ambiguous, and an agent can help with that.

AI agents are a powerful tool to enhance productivity. With the right planning, you can design a system that is both beneficial and practical to your current environment.

#ArtificialIntelligence #WorkflowOptimization #Productivity #TechInsights #AIAgents

I saw an interesting post on Reddit the other day about paying a small fee in order to apply to a job.

I was initially turned off a bit by the subject matter. The job market should always be as open as it can be.

But it got me thinking: what type of principles should be considered in designing for the modern job search?

Now I’m no recruiter, but the main drawback both sides are currently experiencing is white noise.

Job postings that appear genuine but are just to gauge interest. 

Recruiters are trying to sift through hundreds of resumes. Some that seem real but are fluffed up by AI tailoring.

The natural solution is more emphasis on personal verification.

I’m not just referring to networking either.

Portfolios, certifications, verified degrees, and location checks. 

All things that add up to say “Hey, I’m real and exactly who you need”.

AI may stay, but backed-up credibility gives more weight to evaluations.

It’s not outside the realm of feasibility either. 

Verification tools for people and businesses are there. 

Limiting IPs for the scope of your job posting is there. 

It’s just a matter of proper execution.

Job postings don’t need a fee. They just need clarity and trust.

AI may accelerate you, but it can’t redefine you

We have all seen some variation of the following phrases lately:

“Learn AI or you will be left behind.”
“You won’t be replaced by AI, but the person who uses it will”

And I partially agree with the sentiment. 

I do think we need broader acceptance of AI adoption. You can’t exactly close Pandora’s box.

But there’s a nuance often missed in those statements: AI transforms how we work, not who we are.

We all interact with LLMs in our special ways. 

Contexts of our actions may change, but the outlook we bring remains the same.

Where people used Chegg, they now use ChatGPT.

Where someone borrowed from StackOverflow, they now turn to GitHub Copilot

Cutting corners looks different with AI, but it is largely the same habit. 

It’s all about the attitude we take to our workflow.

So the thing that is leaving you behind isn’t exactly prompt engineering, but an adaptive mindset.

AI is an amplifier, not a measure of productivity. 

You can provide value without AI. You can also do a disservice with AI. 

Only you can define who you are.

Optimization is like sharpening a knife: practical at first, but dangerous if overdone.

The ability to take apart a system and reduce its inefficiencies is always a worthwhile skill.

But even though optimizations can be made, it doesn’t mean they are worth the trade-off.

Gains should always outweigh the costs.

Software development has many examples where gains and losses are constantly being evaluated.

How many coding hours need to have been invested before time saved becomes time lost?

Is the process you are trying to optimize going to radically improve the feature’s usage?

Likewise, think of the practical side of software:

Code shouldn’t just be smart. It needs to be something understandable.

An ultra-efficient function that only you would be able to know how to use is not optimization; it is a liability to a well-maintained system.

Optimization should make a system easier, not tedious to work with. 

Of course, that’s not to say it’s an entirely zero-sum game.

The real question with optimization isn’t just right away; it’s about the long-term benefit.

That’s why, before taking the steps to optimize, ask yourself: how sharp can things get before you end up hurting yourself?

#Optimization #SoftwareDevelopment #ProblemSolving #CleanCode #SystemsThinking

Here is an underrated benefit when it comes to using metaphors:

Metaphors are a powerful tool to break down complex problems.

By resorting to universal experiences, you bridge the gap between technical and non-technical people.

But do you realize that an abstract bridge cannot just be for connection, but for reflection?

Think about how complex systems can be. To choose the right metaphor, you need to consider the context.

The context can stem from how your system breaks down, and also understanding who your target audience is.

Many systems have overarching patterns. Especially in software, where you can link universal concepts such as queues and trees to real-world concepts everyone knows.

By trying to pinpoint the right metaphor to your audience, you subconsciously sort out what the major patterns are and how to best explain them.

Additionally, consider what it means to have an isolated representation of your system. 

By abstracting technical details, the metaphor can serve as a guide. The metaphor will allow you to pull out new ideas based on what everyone knows about the metaphor.

Metaphors are beneficial to simplify complex concepts. With the right metaphor, anyone is able to take apart the system and guide it towards a new direction.

Stop asking LLMs for answers when you don’t know the right questions. 

There is a dangerous trap you can find yourself in when using AI. 

You ask a question. 

You get some results back. 

If it’s not to your liking, just feed the output back into the AI with a new question.

And sure, this method can sometimes give the right answer. 

But is it truly the answer you want? 

Let's look at this logistically. 

Prompts. Should. Not. Be. Mindless. 

If you are just going through the motions, letting AI interpret what you want, how do you know you are finding what you truly need? 

Additionally, think about how your results might diverge from what you intended. 

If you don’t have a clear goal in mind, you are just going in circles, hoping the right answer will present itself. 

It’s similar to using Google. 

Yes, you can simply search for terms until you find what you want. 

Or you can learn the proper strategies to get the results you want more efficiently. 

This includes narrowing the scope of what you want as well as not accepting the first result as the whole truth. 

Using LLMs doesn’t have to be tedious. 

With the right practice, anyone can ask the prompts to get the results they desire.

“Aspiring Software Developer”
“Aspiring Data Analyst”

You don’t need to have a specific job title to embody the characteristics of that job.

Take those two headlines I just gave of tech-oriented roles.

Well, there you go.  You are not just aspiring to be in tech. 

You are in tech.

It’s not a demonstration; it’s a barrier.

You can’t just say you are aspiring to be something; you need tangible action.

If you have that action, why not confidently claim the title you want?

Don’t hide your pursuits behind the aspiring wall.

The most underrated skill in designing AI systems: knowing when to say “No”.

In order for AI systems to function, we need to establish patterns. 

We establish these patterns by feeding in large amounts of data.

Feeding in large amounts of data raises two questions:

Is this data credible? 

What value can be derived from this information?

The value we get out of any knowledge isn’t just that it’s right, but how we know something is right.

So that’s why when I think of the future of AI, it isn’t just in the builders, but in the curators. 

Curators who are masters of a domain can guide AI toward specific outcomes in their given topic.

These are people who understand the systematic process and can distinguish facts from falsehoods within AI models.

I’m not just talking about developers either.

All fields, from the sciences to the arts, have specialized expertise that enhances domain credibility.

Because that’s where true knowledge gets determined.

Not in abstract logic, but well-supported truths.

Does that require more coordination and setup? Definitely.

But will it lead to more reliable outcomes? Absolutely.

AI skills shouldn’t just be about building systems, but designing the process surrounding them.

AI models keep getting more powerful.

They are the ones that matter to you, and that’s what counts at the end of the day.

Start small, focus on what matters, and just see where it takes you.

You don’t train AI to replace thought. You train it to augment it.

Too much emphasis is placed on AI replacing work rather than seeing it as creating natural extensions for work as a whole.

The whole “AI will take my job” narrative is built on seeing work as a fixed, immovable unit.

Take software for example:

AI’s capabilities for programming keep getting better.

We see many tools wanting to integrate LLMs into day-to-day coding.

But… companies still want to hire developers.

Why? Because coding is just the baseline.

These models are good at well-defined problems.

But complex system logic and areas of ambiguity?

That is where you need an expert to step in to sort out the logic.

LLMs’ level of memory and context isn’t at that stage yet.

The value of AI will always be linked to how we can automate what’s basic so we can focus on higher levels of logic.

Moreover, think about the value of a worker.

A developer doesn’t just get paid to write software.

They get paid for their perspective, their adaptability, and seeing intuitively beyond what is in front of them.

It’s not as simple as just replacing people with AI.

You need to consider the larger picture of how workflows change and evolve over time.

So are workflows changing as a result of AI? Definitely.

But rather than worry about replacement, let AI elevate your work to new levels of insight.

Most people think prompts are instructions. They’re actually negotiations.

When you send a prompt to an LLM, your response isn’t in absolutes.

There is always a set of contextual rules and tradeoffs that it needs to observe.

Think about how instructions and negotiations work in practice:

If I told you to stack the chairs, that would be a command.

You can stack no chairs, all the chairs, or some of the chairs.

The point being: it’s very defined, either chairs get stacked or not.

Meanwhile, if I told you to “spice up the presentation”:

That can mean multiple things, from stronger visuals, better content, and also altering your tone of voice.

It’s not a single, discrete idea. There is variability; it’s a negotiation.

AI works the same way.

Every prompt isn’t just words. 

It involves comparing those words against patterns to determine what the response needs.

Even a simple direct prompt like “fix this bug” has a degree of interpretation that is essentially a silent negotiation.

Most people think AI prompts are simply instructing the system what to do. 

When in reality, they bargain with an LLM over what matters to them the most.

What’s one recent interaction with an LLM where you treated your words more like a negotiation than an instruction?

Who’s really using ChatGPT?

OpenAI recently posted a study examining ChatGPT usage in collaboration with Duke and Harvard Universities.

Here are some insights you need to know:
 
I) AI is for everybody.

It takes a while to show the true demographic of a product.

Early adoption was skewed toward men in wealthy countries.

Over time, that gap has closed, with 48% of users having a typical feminine name as of July 2025. 

Additionally, the paper highlights the unprecedented growth in countries with a GDP per capita of $10,000 to $40,000, underscoring ChatGPT’s reach from novelty to a widespread societal tool.

II) Non-technical users also matter.

Technical usage with ChatGPT is somewhat limited.

Programming, mathematics, and data analytics account for less than 8% of messages examined.

Now part of that is due to the wide range of other tools available:

Claude, Cursor, Microsoft Copilot.

But I think it also reinforces how we need to handle confirmation bias.

I surround myself with technical people, but that doesn’t mean non-technical people aren’t there.

We need to design AI systems that all can use, not just the select few.

III) AI is not just for work.

ChatGPT had growth in non-work messages, increasing from 53% to over 70% in the study period.

It’s interesting how the paper directly points out how it’s not new users that are changing this metric; it’s existing users growing to accept non-work usage over time.

And that’s a powerful idea with AI adoption as well.

So much of the narrative with AI is on automating jobs, when there are many ways people can use AI to enhance their personal lives.

Just like with coding, a little prompting can do wonders for enabling automation with the average person.

Overall, this paper provided a look into the overarching patterns of AI usage and how there's a broader role to play with LLMs, beyond automating tasks away.

We shut down our thinking before it has time to grow:

“Is this really worth it to build?”

Are you an LLM asker or an LLM doer?

A recent paper conducted by OpenAI examined a portion of ChatGPT messages to see how people are using the model.

By their estimates using messages in the study period:

49% are asking(requesting information or guidance)
40% are doing (requesting a task like writing, coding, etc)
11% are expressing(thoughts and feelings without an action)

Even though doing produces tangible value, it slightly lags behind asking.

Professions like developers or marketers may lean toward doing, but no profession is purely one or the other.

That’s why, when examining AI workflows, I think it’s important to maintain a balance of both asking and doing.

Too much asking without action generates nothing. Too much doing without insight produces shallow results.

Asking and doing may be opposite in spirit, but they are complements that build off each other.

I believe good AI systems understand the push and pull these concepts have in order to produce better outputs.

So, whether you ask LLM for information or ask LLM to do tasks, one thing remains clear:

We may ask different questions, but the thirst for knowledge is universal.

Do you believe you send LLMs more asking messages, doing messages, or a healthy balance of both?

We think AI reinvents workflows, but it’s a mirror reflecting how we already work.

The quest to throw AI into everything has people reexamining workflow systems.

But part of what makes workflow systems so profound isn’t in cornering complex outliers; 

It’s the day-to-day routines.


Designing new habits isn’t always the answer.

We iterate on existing ones based on what we discover.

Overengineering doesn’t produce a good AI workflow.

Simplifying logic into processes does.


Think of how we’ve been processing human workflows already with software:

Code is the communication channel connecting human thinking to machine logic.

AI widens the channel of how these concepts interact with each other.

Processing steps become more ambiguous.

But widening the scope gives interactions more weight in solving direct problems.

Ultimately, these end-to-end interactions are what make workflows possible.

Workflows aren’t just going from A to B; 

They involve understanding all the connection points in between.


Moreover, communication is the baseline for any good workflow.

Workflows function best with defined rules and context.

And how do the models behind AI workflows work best?

By patterns built on rules and context set beforehand.


AI can’t define its own workflow. 

We define the process based on what we know about work itself. 


So don't consider AI workflows as an abstract concept.

Think of them as evolved reflections of what we understand work to be.


How do you define work in today’s fast-moving AI environment?

We think creative prompts are simple. In reality, they’re quite complex.


For some, the point of prompting is quite rigid.

You send the text in, and you get the response out.

But when it comes to subjects like writing and coding, creativity is not a one-off spark.


Creativity has a voice. 

It’s not an input-output relationship.

It’s the back-and-forth link between what you know and what you want to discover.

If responses aren’t refined, the outputs all look the same.


Consider the design in AI-generated photos.

AI can generate photos from many different styles:

Ghibli, Disney, Simpsons.

Can AI represent an aesthetic well? Sure.

But does it capture the creative process within art? Debatable.


We make art by absorbing what we know from others.

Yet there is a clear line between inspiration and plagiarism.


People put their heart and soul into making aesthetics meaningful.

Patterns are present; some spanning decades, others echoing generations.

We shouldn’t summarize a lifetime of work in a few short words.


That’s not to say we can’t use AI for creative pursuits.

We just need to define the patterns through our own unique voices.


So don’t treat creativity in prompts as a backdrop.

Treat it as the main character.
